newsitem.title: UK: Sears wrongfooted on shoes. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sears wrongfooted on shoes. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]

text.p: Shoe shops are no longer the most obvious place to buy shoes, as Britain's leading shoe retailer British Shoe Corporation (BSC), owned by Sears Plc, has found to its cost.
Fewer people are buying footwear in traditional shoe stores.

Instead they are heading off to sportswear retailers for the latest fashion in trainers and street hiking boots or buying shoes where they get their clothes at fashion outlets such as Next Plc and River Island (corrects to make clear Next Plc and River Island are separate companies).
Britain's leading clothing retailer, Marks and Spencer Plc, has taken a sizeable chunk of the market since it expanded its shoe ranges, analysts said.
Loss-making BSC remains the market leader with about 10 percent but has seen its position squeezed by fierce competition.
Last year it made a trading loss of 9.1 million pounds ($14.8 million) after a profit of 7.5 million the previous year.
Sears on Tuesday said a disappointing performance from its Shoe Express and Shoe City plus poor market conditions contributed to its problems.
"In the second half of the year the market once again declined significantly," it said in a statement with its results.
"Surplus stock and in many cases inappropriate product led to substantial markdowns," Sears said.
BSC's troubles have been a persistent drag on parent company Sears, which has just announced the rationalisation of BSC as part of a break-up of its retail empire.
Previous attempts by Sears to shake up BSC have not worked. Analysts said its strategy to emphasise the middle and lower end of the shoe market meant BSC missed out on the boom in branded footwear.
Growing demand for branded products at the higher end of the market has favoured specialist and fashion shops, while Marks and Spencer has been cleaning up in the middle, they said.
"Any buoyancy in the shoe market has been creamed off by non-specialists," said Robert Clarke of retail research group Corporate Intelligence.
Sears, striving to inject new life into loss-hit BSC, got rid of many of its retail fascias and introduced Shoe Express and Shoe City, aimed at the bottom end of the shoe market.
But these have not done well because they have lacked the "aspirational" brands that have become so desirable.
"Shoe Express is very price-driven but today's consumer is looking for something different," said Clive Vaughan at Verdict Research.
He said although the overall shoe market was growing at a reasonable rate, the traditional shoe specialists were trending downwards and underperforming the market.
He said BSC's problems were to a degree self-inflicted because it had never fully exploited its dominant market position.
Sears has finally decided to get to grips with the problem, appointing corporate rescue specialist David James to deal with BSC.
He will decide whether to sell BSC's shops or find ways for them to share in some form of recovery without further investment.
"Consideration will also be given to retaining businesses or assets which could enhance our clothing businesses," Sears said.
BSC currently has 330 Shoe Express stores, 81 out-of-town Shoe City outlets, 140 Dolcis and Cable & Co shops, plus 226 concessions in 16 department stores.
The rationalisation of BSC forms part of a break-up of Sears, including the demerger of Selfridges, its London department store. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
